## "Was that a Required control, or an Addressable one?"

Your Quality Analyst (QA) is back, and she's narrowed the question. The minimum-necessary finding
from `the-hipaa-privacy-rule` is logged — three of the extract's six fields didn't need to be
there. The covered-entity premise from `information-governance-in-a-covered-entity` is adopted.
Neither of those settles the question she actually walked in with: "Before we even get to whether
this is a breach — was the Brookfield laptop *supposed* to be encrypted? Not 'was Lakeshore's
policy reasonable.' I mean: under HIPAA's own rule, was encryption a flat requirement we failed,
or something else?"

It's the right question to ask before the breach question, not after. The systems administrator
has already told you what he can and can't confirm: the laptop was enrolled under Lakeshore's
full-disk-encryption policy, auto-enforced at enrollment — but a device-management platform
migration left this specific device's encryption-status field reading "not reported," neither on
nor off, for the exact window spanning the migration and the loss. Nobody can say, today, whether
encryption was actually running on that device when it went missing.

That's not a question `the-hipaa-privacy-rule` can answer — it governs use and disclosure, not
safeguards. It's not `breach-notification-and-dual-reporting`'s question either — that module runs
the four-factor breach test, and it needs this module's answer as an input, not the other way
around. This module owns exactly one thing: what the HIPAA Security Rule's own safeguards
required of that laptop, and whether Lakeshore's encryption posture — and its gap — is a
compliance problem in its own right, independent of whatever module 4 eventually decides about the
breach itself.

## Why this rule exists, and the ITSM bridge

The HIPAA Privacy Rule, which the last module covered, answers "who's allowed to see this and for
what reason." The Security Rule answers a different question: once PHI (protected health
information) exists electronically, what actually has to stand between it and the people who
aren't allowed to see it, or the failure that destroys or corrupts it. The failure mode the
Security Rule exists to prevent isn't a nurse browsing a chart out of curiosity — that's a Privacy
Rule problem. It's an unencrypted laptop in the back seat of a car, a terminated employee's login
still working two months after the exit interview, a server with no audit log admitting nobody
knows who touched what. Confidentiality, integrity, and availability — lose any one of them and a
donor-eligibility record becomes untrustworthy, exposed, or gone.

You already run a version of this discipline. `grc-frameworks-and-risk-management` built a full
categorize → select → implement → assess → authorize → monitor cycle, and showed you a POA&M
(plan of action and milestones) tracking a control implemented and documented but not yet exercised
on its first scheduled cycle. That cycle's "select" step is where NIST's own tailoring guidance
lets an organization choose a compensating control instead of a baseline one, document why, and
move on. That's the same shape you're about to read in 164.306(d): an "Addressable" implementation
specification isn't a control you can skip — it's one where the organization has to show its work,
assess it, implement it if reasonable, or document why not and substitute something equivalent. The
paperwork differs; the discipline is the same risk-based tailoring decision you've already learned
to defend.

## The rule in plain English

Start with what every covered entity has to do, full stop, no tailoring available: 164.306(a)
requires ensuring the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of all electronic PHI the
organization creates, receives, maintains, or transmits; protecting against reasonably anticipated
threats; protecting against impermissible uses or disclosures; and ensuring workforce compliance.
That's the destination. Everything in 164.308, 164.310, and 164.312 is a means to that end, and
164.306(b) explicitly lets a covered entity choose *how* to get there — any security measure that
reasonably and appropriately implements the standards, sized to the organization's own scale, tech
stack, cost constraints, and actual risk.

Then comes the mechanism that decides how much flexibility exists for any *specific* control:
164.306(d)'s Required/Addressable split. If an implementation specification is labeled "Required,"
there's no judgment call — implement it. If it's labeled "Addressable," the organization must (1)
assess whether that specification is a reasonable and appropriate safeguard given its own
environment, and then either (2a) implement it if the assessment says yes, or (2b) if not, document
*why* it isn't reasonable and appropriate, and implement an equivalent alternative measure if one
is reasonable and appropriate. Read that again, because it's the single most commonly
misunderstood sentence in this whole subpart: "Addressable" is not a synonym for "optional." It's a
mandatory *process* — assess, then implement-or-substitute-and-document — attached to a control
whose *outcome* has some flexibility. Skipping the process entirely, with no assessment and no
documentation, satisfies nothing.

164.312(a)(2)(iv) — encryption and decryption of electronic PHI — is labeled Addressable. That one
fact is the hinge this whole module turns on, for the laptop and for every other Addressable
specification in 164.308, 164.310, and 164.312.

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| 45 CFR 164.306(a) | "One-sixty-four point three-oh-six, paragraph a" | The overall standard: ensure confidentiality, integrity, and availability of e-PHI; protect against reasonably anticipated threats and impermissible disclosures; ensure workforce compliance. | The outcome every safeguard below exists to serve — and the standard a documented-but-unverified control can still fail even if its own paperwork is clean. |
| 45 CFR 164.306(d) | "Paragraph d" | Defines Required vs. Addressable implementation specifications, and spells out the Addressable process: assess, then implement, or document why not and substitute an equivalent measure. | The mechanism that decides whether the laptop's encryption gap is a paperwork problem or a real one. |
| 45 CFR 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D) | "Three-oh-eight, paragraph a, sub-one, sub-two, sub-D" | Information system activity review (Required): regularly review records of system activity — audit logs, access reports, security incident tracking. | The provision that should have caught an "unreported" encryption-status field before the laptop ever left the building. |
| 45 CFR 164.308(a)(6) | "Paragraph a, sub-six" | Security incident procedures: policies to address security incidents, with a Required specification to identify, respond to, mitigate, and document them. | What's now actually running, because the laptop is missing. |
| 45 CFR 164.310(d)(1)-(2) | "Three-ten, paragraph d" | Device and media controls: policies governing hardware/media carrying e-PHI moving into, out of, and within a facility; disposal and media re-use are Required, accountability and backup-before-movement are Addressable. | Governs exactly the act of a staff member carrying a BECS extract out of Lakeshore's central site on a laptop. |
| 45 CFR 164.312(a)(2)(i) | "Three-twelve, paragraph a, sub-two, sub-one" | Unique user identification (Required): assign each user a unique name or number for identifying and tracking identity. | Compare directly to Part 11's 11.100 uniqueness requirement, below. |
| 45 CFR 164.312(a)(2)(iv) | "Sub-two, sub-four" | Encryption and decryption of e-PHI (Addressable). | The exact specification the laptop's status is genuinely unresolved against. |
| 45 CFR 164.312(b) | "Paragraph b" | Audit controls: hardware/software/procedural mechanisms that record and examine activity in systems holding e-PHI. | Compare directly to Part 11's 11.10(e) audit-trail requirement, below. |
| 45 CFR 164.312(d) | "Paragraph d" | Person or entity authentication: verify that whoever is accessing e-PHI is actually who they claim to be. | Compare directly to Part 11's 11.200 identity-verification components, below. |

## The actual text

All quotes below come verbatim from `sources/cfr/45-164-security-rule-excerpt.md`.

### 164.306 — Security standards: General rules

> (a) General requirements. Covered entities and business associates must do the following:
> (1) Ensure the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of all electronic protected health
> information the covered entity or business associate creates, receives, maintains, or
> transmits.
> (2) Protect against any reasonably anticipated threats or hazards to the security or integrity
> of such information.
> (3) Protect against any reasonably anticipated uses or disclosures of such information that are
> not permitted or required under subpart E of this part.
> (4) Ensure compliance with this subpart by its workforce.
> (b) Flexibility of approach. (1) Covered entities and business associates may use any security
> measures that allow the covered entity or business associate to reasonably and appropriately
> implement the standards and implementation specifications as specified in this subpart.
> (2) In deciding which security measures to use, a covered entity or business associate must take
> into account the following factors: (i) The size, complexity, and capabilities of the covered
> entity or business associate. (ii) The covered entity's or the business associate's technical
> infrastructure, hardware, and software security capabilities. (iii) The costs of security
> measures. (iv) The probability and criticality of potential risks to electronic protected health
> information.
> (c) Standards. A covered entity or business associate must comply with the applicable standards
> as provided in this section and in §§ 164.308, 164.310, 164.312, 164.314 and 164.316 with
> respect to all electronic protected health information.
> (d) Implementation specifications. In this subpart: (1) Implementation specifications are
> required or addressable. If an implementation specification is required, the word "Required"
> appears in parentheses after the title of the implementation specification. If an implementation
> specification is addressable, the word "Addressable" appears in parentheses after the title of
> the implementation specification. (2) When a standard adopted in § 164.308, § 164.310, §
> 164.312, § 164.314, or § 164.316 includes required implementation specifications, a covered
> entity or business associate must implement the implementation specifications. (3) When a
> standard adopted in § 164.308, § 164.310, § 164.312, § 164.314, or § 164.316 includes
> addressable implementation specifications, a covered entity or business associate must— (i)
> Assess whether each implementation specification is a reasonable and appropriate safeguard in
> its environment, when analyzed with reference to the likely contribution to protecting
> electronic protected health information; and (ii) As applicable to the covered entity or
> business associate— (A) Implement the implementation specification if reasonable and
> appropriate; or (B) If implementing the implementation specification is not reasonable and
> appropriate— (1) Document why it would not be reasonable and appropriate to implement the
> implementation specification; and (2) Implement an equivalent alternative measure if reasonable
> and appropriate.
> (e) Maintenance. A covered entity or business associate must review and modify the security
> measures implemented under this subpart as needed to continue provision of reasonable and
> appropriate protection of electronic protected health information, and update documentation of
> such security measures in accordance with § 164.316(b)(2)(iii).

Notice what (d)(3) actually demands, word by word: "assess," then "implement ... or ... document
why ... and implement an equivalent alternative." Three possible honest end-states for an
Addressable specification — implemented, or documented-not-reasonable-with-a-substitute, never a
fourth, silent option of "didn't get to it." And notice (e): the standard isn't a one-time box to
check. Security measures have to be reviewed and modified "as needed," on an ongoing basis — a
Required or satisfied-Addressable control from last year isn't automatically still satisfied this
year.

### 164.308 — Administrative safeguards

> (a) A covered entity or business associate must, in accordance with § 164.306:
> (1)(i) Standard: Security management process. Implement policies and procedures to prevent,
> detect, contain, and correct security violations.
> (ii) Implementation specifications: (A) Risk analysis (Required). Conduct an accurate and
> thorough assessment of the potential risks and vulnerabilities to the confidentiality, integrity,
> and availability of electronic protected health information held by the covered entity or
> business associate. (B) Risk management (Required). Implement security measures sufficient to
> reduce risks and vulnerabilities to a reasonable and appropriate level to comply with §
> 164.306(a). (C) Sanction policy (Required). Apply appropriate sanctions against workforce
> members who fail to comply with the security policies and procedures of the covered entity or
> business associate. (D) Information system activity review (Required). Implement procedures to
> regularly review records of information system activity, such as audit logs, access reports,
> and security incident tracking reports.
> (2) Standard: Assigned security responsibility. Identify the security official who is
> responsible for the development and implementation of the policies and procedures required by
> this subpart for the covered entity or business associate.
> (3)(i) Standard: Workforce security. Implement policies and procedures to ensure that all
> members of its workforce have appropriate access to electronic protected health information, as
> provided under paragraph (a)(4) of this section, and to prevent those workforce members who do
> not have access under paragraph (a)(4) of this section from obtaining access to electronic
> protected health information.
> (ii) Implementation specifications: (A) Authorization and/or supervision (Addressable).
> Implement procedures for the authorization and/or supervision of workforce members who work with
> electronic protected health information or in locations where it might be accessed. (B)
> Workforce clearance procedure (Addressable). Implement procedures to determine that the access
> of a workforce member to electronic protected health information is appropriate. (C) Termination
> procedures (Addressable). Implement procedures for terminating access to electronic protected
> health information when the employment of, or other arrangement with, a workforce member ends or
> as required by determinations made as specified in paragraph (a)(3)(ii)(B) of this section.
> (4)(i) Standard: Information access management. Implement policies and procedures for
> authorizing access to electronic protected health information that are consistent with the
> applicable requirements of subpart E of this part.
> (ii) Implementation specifications: (A) Isolating health care clearinghouse functions
> (Required). If a health care clearinghouse is part of a larger organization, the clearinghouse
> must implement policies and procedures that protect the electronic protected health information
> of the clearinghouse from unauthorized access by the larger organization. (B) Access
> authorization (Addressable). Implement policies and procedures for granting access to electronic
> protected health information, for example, through access to a workstation, transaction,
> program, process, or other mechanism. (C) Access establishment and modification (Addressable).
> Implement policies and procedures that, based upon the covered entity's or the business
> associate's access authorization policies, establish, document, review, and modify a user's
> right of access to a workstation, transaction, program, or process.
> (5)(i) Standard: Security awareness and training. Implement a security awareness and training
> program for all members of its workforce (including management).
> (ii) Implementation specifications. Implement: (A) Security reminders (Addressable). Periodic
> security updates. (B) Protection from malicious software (Addressable). Procedures for guarding
> against, detecting, and reporting malicious software. (C) Log-in monitoring (Addressable).
> Procedures for monitoring log-in attempts and reporting discrepancies. (D) Password management
> (Addressable). Procedures for creating, changing, and safeguarding passwords.
> (6)(i) Standard: Security incident procedures. Implement policies and procedures to address
> security incidents.
> (ii) Implementation specification: Response and reporting (Required). Identify and respond to
> suspected or known security incidents; mitigate, to the extent practicable, harmful effects of
> security incidents that are known to the covered entity or business associate; and document
> security incidents and their outcomes.
> (7)(i) Standard: Contingency plan. Establish (and implement as needed) policies and procedures
> for responding to an emergency or other occurrence (for example, fire, vandalism, system
> failure, and natural disaster) that damages systems that contain electronic protected health
> information.
> (ii) Implementation specifications: (A) Data backup plan (Required). Establish and implement
> procedures to create and maintain retrievable exact copies of electronic protected health
> information. (B) Disaster recovery plan (Required). Establish (and implement as needed)
> procedures to restore any loss of data. (C) Emergency mode operation plan (Required). Establish
> (and implement as needed) procedures to enable continuation of critical business processes for
> protection of the security of electronic protected health information while operating in
> emergency mode. (D) Testing and revision procedures (Addressable). Implement procedures for
> periodic testing and revision of contingency plans. (E) Applications and data criticality
> analysis (Addressable). Assess the relative criticality of specific applications and data in
> support of other contingency plan components.
> (8) Standard: Evaluation. Perform a periodic technical and nontechnical evaluation, based
> initially upon the standards implemented under this rule and, subsequently, in response to
> environmental or operational changes affecting the security of electronic protected health
> information, that establishes the extent to which a covered entity's or business associate's
> security policies and procedures meet the requirements of this subpart.
> (b)(1) Business associate contracts and other arrangements. A covered entity may permit a
> business associate to create, receive, maintain, or transmit electronic protected health
> information on the covered entity's behalf only if the covered entity obtains satisfactory
> assurances, in accordance with § 164.314(a), that the business associate will appropriately
> safeguard the information.

164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D) — information system activity review, Required, no tailoring available — is
worth sitting with before moving on. It obligates Lakeshore to regularly review records of
information system activity: audit logs, access reports, security incident tracking reports. A
device-management platform's own inventory report, showing a device's encryption-status field
as "not reported," is exactly the kind of record this specification requires someone to be
reviewing on a regular cadence — not waiting to discover it only after a laptop goes missing.

### 164.310 — Physical safeguards

> A covered entity or business associate must, in accordance with § 164.306:
> (a)(1) Standard: Facility access controls. Implement policies and procedures to limit physical
> access to its electronic information systems and the facility or facilities in which they are
> housed, while ensuring that properly authorized access is allowed.
> (2) Implementation specifications: (i) Contingency operations (Addressable). Establish (and
> implement as needed) procedures that allow facility access in support of restoration of lost
> data under the disaster recovery plan and emergency mode operations plan in the event of an
> emergency. (ii) Facility security plan (Addressable). Implement policies and procedures to
> safeguard the facility and the equipment therein from unauthorized physical access, tampering,
> and theft. (iii) Access control and validation procedures (Addressable). Implement procedures to
> control and validate a person's access to facilities based on their role or function, including
> visitor control, and control of access to software programs for testing and revision. (iv)
> Maintenance records (Addressable). Implement policies and procedures to document repairs and
> modifications to the physical components of a facility which are related to security (for
> example, hardware, walls, doors, and locks).
> (b) Standard: Workstation use. Implement policies and procedures that specify the proper
> functions to be performed, the manner in which those functions are to be performed, and the
> physical attributes of the surroundings of a specific workstation or class of workstation that
> can access electronic protected health information.
> (c) Standard: Workstation security. Implement physical safeguards for all workstations that
> access electronic protected health information, to restrict access to authorized users.
> (d)(1) Standard: Device and media controls. Implement policies and procedures that govern the
> receipt and removal of hardware and electronic media that contain electronic protected health
> information into and out of a facility, and the movement of these items within the facility.
> (2) Implementation specifications: (i) Disposal (Required). Implement policies and procedures
> to address the final disposition of electronic protected health information, and/or the
> hardware or electronic media on which it is stored. (ii) Media re-use (Required). Implement
> procedures for removal of electronic protected health information from electronic media before
> the media are made available for re-use. (iii) Accountability (Addressable). Maintain a record
> of the movements of hardware and electronic media and any person responsible therefore. (iv)
> Data backup and storage (Addressable). Create a retrievable, exact copy of electronic protected
> health information, when needed, before movement of equipment.

164.310(d) is the physical-safeguard standard most directly on point for a staff member carrying a
BECS extract out of Lakeshore's central site on a laptop in the first place: "device and media
controls" exist precisely to govern hardware "into and out of a facility." Note that accountability
— maintaining a record of who's responsible for hardware as it moves — is itself only Addressable,
not Required. That matters later: Lakeshore can't be faulted under 164.310(d) for failing to track
the laptop's movement unless it either never assessed that specification or assessed it, found it
reasonable, and still didn't implement it.

### 164.312 — Technical safeguards

> A covered entity or business associate must, in accordance with § 164.306:
> (a)(1) Standard: Access control. Implement technical policies and procedures for electronic
> information systems that maintain electronic protected health information to allow access only
> to those persons or software programs that have been granted access rights as specified in §
> 164.308(a)(4).
> (2) Implementation specifications: (i) Unique user identification (Required). Assign a unique
> name and/or number for identifying and tracking user identity. (ii) Emergency access procedure
> (Required). Establish (and implement as needed) procedures for obtaining necessary electronic
> protected health information during an emergency. (iii) Automatic logoff (Addressable).
> Implement electronic procedures that terminate an electronic session after a predetermined time
> of inactivity. (iv) Encryption and decryption (Addressable). Implement a mechanism to encrypt
> and decrypt electronic protected health information.
> (b) Standard: Audit controls. Implement hardware, software, and/or procedural mechanisms that
> record and examine activity in information systems that contain or use electronic protected
> health information.
> (c)(1) Standard: Integrity. Implement policies and procedures to protect electronic protected
> health information from improper alteration or destruction.
> (2) Implementation specification: Mechanism to authenticate electronic protected health
> information (Addressable). Implement electronic mechanisms to corroborate that electronic
> protected health information has not been altered or destroyed in an unauthorized manner.
> (d) Standard: Person or entity authentication. Implement procedures to verify that a person or
> entity seeking access to electronic protected health information is the one claimed.
> (e)(1) Standard: Transmission security. Implement technical security measures to guard against
> unauthorized access to electronic protected health information that is being transmitted over an
> electronic communications network.
> (2) Implementation specifications: (i) Integrity controls (Addressable). Implement security
> measures to ensure that electronically transmitted electronic protected health information is
> not improperly modified without detection until disposed of. (ii) Encryption (Addressable).
> Implement a mechanism to encrypt electronic protected health information whenever deemed
> appropriate.

And there it is, inside 164.312(a)(2): unique user identification is **Required**; encryption and
decryption of e-PHI is **Addressable**. Same paragraph, same standard, two completely different
compliance postures for two different controls sitting right next to each other.

## Mapping this against Part 11, honestly

`data-integrity-and-records`'s `audit-trails-and-esignatures` module already taught 11.10, 11.50,
11.70, 11.100, 11.200, and 11.300 in full depth — none of that gets re-quoted here. What's worth
building is an honest comparison, because the overlap is real and so is the difference, and
flattening either one into "basically the same rule" would be wrong.

| HIPAA Security Rule | Part 11 (reference only) | The real overlap | The real difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| 164.312(a)(2)(i), unique user identification (Required) | 11.100(a), each signature unique to one individual, never reused or reassigned | Both demand one identity, one accountable person, never shared or recycled credentials. | 164.312(a)(2)(i) is about system *access* broadly; 11.100 is specifically about the identity behind a *signature*. Related controls, not the same control. |
| 164.312(b), audit controls | 11.10(e), secure, computer-generated, time-stamped audit trail | Both require a mechanism that records and lets you reconstruct who did what, when, to data that matters. | 164.312(b) exists to protect PHI confidentiality/integrity generally; 11.10(e) exists specifically to prove a CGMP record wasn't altered without a trace. Same mechanism, different regulated interest behind it. |
| 164.312(d), person or entity authentication | 11.200, two distinct identification components for a non-biometric signature | Both require verifying that whoever is acting is actually who they claim to be, not assumed. | 164.312(d) is a general login/access standard; 11.200 is narrower and stricter — it specifically requires *signature execution* to use two components and be collusion-resistant, not just login. |

**The one genuine structural difference, stated plainly: Part 11 has no Required/Addressable
concept at all.** Every Part 11 control this curriculum has taught — 11.10(e)'s audit trail,
11.50's signature manifestation, 11.70's tamper-resistant linkage, 11.100's uniqueness, 11.200's
two-component execution, 11.300's password controls — simply applies, in full, to any system that
falls under Part 11's scope, or it doesn't apply at all (the system is outside Part 11's scope, or
the enforcement-discretion question `audit-trails-and-esignatures` already walked through for
11.10(e) specifically). There is no Part 11 mechanism that says "assess whether 11.300(b)'s
password-revision requirement is reasonable for your environment, and if not, document why and
substitute something equivalent." If 11.300(b) applies, Lakeshore revises passwords periodically,
full stop. HIPAA's Security Rule, by contrast, builds that exact assess-or-substitute process
directly into roughly half its implementation specifications. That's not a loophole HIPAA built in
by accident — 164.306(b)(2) says plainly that a covered entity's size, infrastructure, and cost
constraints are legitimate factors in choosing *how* to meet a standard. Part 11 was written for a
narrower, more homogeneous universe of CGMP record-keeping systems; HIPAA's Security Rule was
written to reach everything from a solo practitioner's laptop to a multi-hospital health system,
and the Required/Addressable split is how it does that without either over-specifying small
operations or under-specifying large ones.

Don't let that difference collapse into "HIPAA is more lenient." It isn't — 164.306(d)(3)'s process
for an Addressable specification is itself mandatory, and skipping it (no assessment, no
documentation, no substitute) is every bit as much a finding as failing a Part 11 Required control
outright. The two rules also aren't protecting the same thing: Part 11 exists to make an electronic
record or signature trustworthy enough to stand in for paper in an FDA-regulated record-keeping
system; HIPAA's Security Rule exists to keep PHI confidential, intact, and available, regardless of
whether it ever touches a signature or a CGMP record. They overlap hard on access control and audit
logging because both care about "who touched this and can we prove it" — but one is answering "is
this signature legally binding" and the other is answering "is this information still safe."

## Resolving the encryption question — a Security Rule question, not the breach question

Now apply all of this to the one open fact module 1 locked and left open: the laptop's encryption
status.

**Step one: classify the control.** 164.312(a)(2)(iv), encryption and decryption of e-PHI, is
labeled Addressable in the text just quoted. Not Required. There is no blanket HIPAA mandate that
every laptop holding e-PHI must be encrypted.

**Step two: was Lakeshore's policy itself a sound response to 164.306(d)(3)?** Yes — and this is
worth crediting plainly, the same way `the-hipaa-privacy-rule` credited a clean pass on 11.200 in
a prior module rather than treating every finding as a gap. Lakeshore assessed that full-disk
encryption is a reasonable and appropriate safeguard for laptops carrying e-PHI (an assessment any
competent risk analysis would reach, given how often laptops are lost or stolen relative to
servers sitting in a locked facility), and it implemented that assessment as a standing policy:
full-disk encryption required on every end-user laptop, auto-enforced through central device
management at the moment of enrollment. That's exactly the Addressable process working as
designed — assess, then implement, not implement-by-default and not skip-and-hope. **By policy,
Lakeshore's posture on this Addressable specification is sound.**

**Step three — and this is the real finding — a sound policy is not the same thing as a satisfied
164.306(a).** The systems administrator can confirm the laptop was enrolled under the encryption
policy. He cannot confirm, for this specific device, that full-disk encryption was actually active
when it went missing, because a device-management platform migration left exactly this unit's
encryption-status field reading "not reported" for the relevant window. That is not a policy
failure. It's a verification and monitoring failure, and it sits squarely on 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D) —
the Required specification obligating Lakeshore to regularly review records of information system
activity. An encryption-status field stuck at "not reported" is precisely the kind of record that
specification exists to catch, and catch *before* the device is gone, not after. 164.306(a)(1)'s
own overall mandate — ensure the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of e-PHI — isn't
satisfied by a well-reasoned Addressable-specification decision sitting in a policy binder if
nobody can confirm, for an actual device, that the control it describes actually ran.

This is the same pattern this curriculum has flagged before, in a different system, for a
different reason: `audit-trails-and-esignatures` found a Part 11 password-revision policy that was
written correctly but never verified as actually enforced — "the policy was written. It was never
technically enforced. Nobody circled back to confirm the system was doing what the document said
it would." The Brookfield laptop's encryption gap is the same shape, wearing different clothes: a
policy that reads well, and no evidence the control it describes was confirmed operating on this
one device, at the one moment it mattered.

**State the finding precisely, because modules 4 and 5 build directly on exactly this wording and
nothing broader:** Lakeshore has a genuine Security Rule compliance gap in *how it verifies that
an Addressable control it chose to implement actually operated on a given device* — a
monitoring/verification gap under 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D), sitting on top of an otherwise reasonable
164.306(d)(3) decision about encryption itself. **This finding says nothing about whether a breach
occurred.** Whether unencrypted PHI was actually acquired, viewed, or exfiltrated by whoever has
that laptop now is 164.402's own four-factor test — a completely separate question that turns on
facts (was the data actually accessed, who has the device now, what's the nature and extent of the
PHI involved) this module doesn't have and isn't trying to reason through. `breach-notification-
and-dual-reporting` picks that up next, carrying this exact, narrow finding forward as one input
among several, not as a predetermined verdict.

## What an inspector or reviewer would actually look for

An OCR (Office for Civil Rights) investigator wouldn't ask "do you have an encryption policy" —
every organization being investigated has a policy. They'd ask for the 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A) risk
analysis that led Lakeshore to treat encryption as reasonable and appropriate in the first place,
the 164.306(d)(3) documentation of that assessment, and then — separately — the device-level
evidence that encryption was actually active on *this* laptop at the relevant time: a management
console's status log, a compliance report, anything beyond the policy document itself. Right now,
Lakeshore has the first two. It doesn't have the third, for this one device, because the migration
left that field blank. A bad answer sounds like "our policy requires full-disk encryption on every
laptop." A credible answer produces the device's own status history, not just the policy that was
supposed to produce it.

## Common traps

**"Addressable means optional."** This is the trap the whole module exists to refute. 164.306(d)(3)
makes the process itself mandatory — assess, then implement or document-and-substitute. An
organization that never assessed an Addressable specification at all, and has nothing on file
explaining why, has failed 164.306(d)(3) regardless of whether the underlying control would have
turned out to be reasonable.

**"We have a policy that covers this, so we're compliant."** Also the trap this module's own
finding refutes directly. A sound 164.306(d)(3) decision, properly documented, is necessary but not
sufficient. 164.306(a)'s overall confidentiality/integrity/availability mandate is a standing,
ongoing obligation — satisfied only when there's evidence the control the policy describes is
actually operating, not merely written down. A policy document proves intent. A device's own status
log proves compliance.

## What this means for your job

- **Before you accept "it's Addressable" as the end of a conversation, ask for the 164.306(d)(3)
  paperwork.** An Addressable specification never formally assessed, with no documented reasoning
  on file, is a finding — whether or not the underlying control happens to be in place.
- **Separate "is our policy reasonable" from "can we prove it ran on this device."** Different
  questions, different evidence. Make sure someone is answering both, per device, not just citing
  the fleet-wide policy.
- **Treat an "unreported" or "unknown" status field as a finding the moment you see it, not after a
  device goes missing.** 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D) obligates regular review of exactly this kind of
  record. A migration that silently breaks status reporting on even one device is worth escalating
  immediately, not discovering during an incident review.
- **When comparing "HIPAA-compliant" and "Part 11-compliant" claims, ask which specific controls
  they mean.** The access-control and audit-logging overlap is real, but satisfying 11.100's
  signature-uniqueness requirement doesn't automatically satisfy 164.312(a)(2)(i)'s broader access
  standard, or vice versa — adjacent controls, not identical ones.
- **Don't let this module's finding slide into a breach conclusion.** The verification gap is real
  and logged. Whether it adds up to a reportable breach is 164.402's four-factor test, next module,
  and it needs facts this module doesn't have.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Does HIPAA's Security Rule flatly require every laptop holding e-PHI to be encrypted?

No — and this is worth holding onto precisely. 164.312(a)(2)(iv), encryption and decryption of
e-PHI, is explicitly labeled **Addressable**, not Required. There is no blanket HIPAA mandate that
every device be encrypted. What *is* mandatory is the 164.306(d)(3) process attached to that
Addressable label: assess whether encryption is reasonable and appropriate in your environment,
then implement it if so, or document why not and substitute something equivalent. Lakeshore's
policy of auto-enforcing full-disk encryption at enrollment is one way of discharging that process
soundly — but it's a reasonable choice within a flexible requirement, not evidence of an absolute
rule that doesn't exist in the text.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: If Lakeshore's encryption policy was itself reasonable and properly documented, is there still a Security Rule compliance problem with the Brookfield laptop?

Yes — and this is this module's central, locked finding. A sound 164.306(d)(3) decision about the
*policy* doesn't satisfy 164.306(a)'s ongoing mandate to actually ensure confidentiality,
integrity, and availability for *this device*. The device-management migration left this laptop's
encryption-status field "not reported," and nobody can currently confirm encryption was active on
it when it went missing. That's a monitoring/verification gap tied to 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D)'s
Required information-system-activity-review specification — a real, separate compliance problem
sitting on top of an otherwise sound policy decision. It is not, on its own, a determination that a
breach occurred; that's 164.402's four-factor test, taken up next module.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: Part 11 has strict controls for electronic signatures. Does Part 11 have its own "Addressable" category the way HIPAA's Security Rule does, for a control a regulated company judges isn't reasonable in its environment?

No. This is the one genuine structural difference this module insists on naming honestly: Part 11,
as taught in full in `data-integrity-and-records`, has no Required/Addressable concept anywhere in
its text. 11.10(e)'s audit trail, 11.50's signature manifestation, 11.70's tamper-resistant
linkage, 11.100's uniqueness, 11.200's two-component execution, and 11.300's password controls each
simply apply, in full, to a system within Part 11's scope, or they don't apply because the system
or the specific clause falls outside that scope (or inside FDA's own stated enforcement-discretion
list, a separate and narrower question `audit-trails-and-esignatures` already covered). There's no
Part 11 mechanism letting an organization assess a control, decide it's not reasonable for its
environment, and substitute something equivalent instead. HIPAA's Security Rule built that
flexibility in on purpose; Part 11 did not.
:::

## Where this goes next

The Security Rule side of this incident is now reasoned through: Lakeshore's encryption policy was
a sound response to an Addressable specification, but a real, specific verification gap means
nobody can confirm that policy actually operated on the one device that matters. That finding —
not a breach determination, just a safeguards gap — is now the locked input `breach-notification-
and-dual-reporting` picks up next, where 164.402's four-factor test finally asks the question this
module deliberately didn't: given everything now known, and everything still genuinely unresolved,
did a reportable breach of unsecured PHI actually occur — and does it also trigger FDA's own,
separate 45-day BPDR clock alongside HIPAA's 60-day one?
